opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing missing is a goal. To have a prior, you need something the prior is a prior *about*, some ground truth you'll later learn from. In reinforcement learning, there's a right thing to do: the thing that gets you reward. You take an action, you see what happens, and you can tell whether it was good or bad. That's what makes learning from experience possible. You can be wrong, and you can find out you were wrong.

Large language models don't have that. They're trained to predict what a person would say next. That's not the same as predicting what will happen in the world. They have no substantive goal, and so there's no sense in which one thing they say is right and another is wrong, except relative to what people tended to write. If you have no goal, you can't have a prior about how to achieve it, because there's no feedback that tells you whether you're doing better.

People say, "Okay, but they have all this knowledge, so surely it's a good starting point, and then we'll add experience on top." But I'm skeptical of that framing. Mimicking people is a different kind of thing from understanding the world. A model that predicts what a person would say isn't surprised when the world does something unexpected, and it doesn't adjust when it is. It isn't modeling the consequences of its actions. It's modeling people's text.

And I'd point to nature. Animals don't learn by imitation, not primarily. A squirrel isn't being shown what to do and copying it. Infants aren't really imitating either; they're trying things, waving their hands, moving their eyes, and seeing what happens. Supervised learning, learning from examples of the correct answer, basically doesn't occur in nature. What occurs is learning from experience: you act, you observe consequences, you get some signal of how well it went.

So my worry is that by starting from imitation, you're building on the wrong foundation. There's this recurring lesson, the bitter lesson, that approaches leaning on human knowledge do well at first, then get overtaken by methods that scale with computation and experience. I expect that's what will happen here. Systems that learn from experience, from a stream of action, observation, and reward, will eventually outdo systems that start from human data, and people who've invested in the imitation approach will find it hard to let go of.

r001.rationale: It says a prior needs something to be about, namely ground truth the learner can later learn from.

r002.rationale: It argues that without a substantive goal, there is no goal-based sense in which one thing the model says is right and another is wrong.

r003.rationale: It states that in reinforcement learning, the right action is the one that gets reward.

r004.rationale: It describes observing outcomes and reward after acting, but does not say that predictions in a world model can be checked against what subsequently happens.

r005.rationale: It says the model does not predict world outcomes or model action consequences, but does not specify a lack of predictions about how an interlocutor responds to the model's own utterances.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd push back on the premise a little. I don't think of what large language models do as imitation learning in the way it's usually meant, but let's take the question as it's asked. The claim is that by predicting what people would say, you get a prior, and then you can learn from experience on top of that. My concern is that it's not clear what the prior is a prior for.

To learn from experience, you need a goal. You need some notion of what's good and what's bad, some sense of the consequences of what you do, so you can be surprised when the world doesn't go the way you expected and adjust. A language model doesn't have that. It has a model of what a person would say next. That's not a model of the world. It doesn't predict what will happen, it predicts what someone would write. And there's no ground truth about what someone would write. There's no right thing to say. So there's nothing for the system to be surprised about, nothing that tells it it was wrong, except in the sense that a different token appeared.

Compare that to an animal, or a reinforcement learning agent. It acts, something happens, it gets a reward or it doesn't, and it has a model that predicts what would happen, so it can be wrong and correct itself. That's the basic loop. That's the thing that scales with experience, because experience is unlimited. The web is not unlimited. Human-generated text is one-off data. You can't act and get more of it.

So when people say the language model is a prior for learning from experience, I'd ask: what's the knowledge in it? It's knowledge about how people talk. That's a knowledge of people, not of the world. And it isn't organized around a goal, so when you later try to attach a goal to it, you're bolting the important thing on at the end. I think the important thing should come first. The goal, the model of consequences, the ability to be wrong. That's what the squirrel has, that's what a child has before they can speak, and that's the thing I'd want to build on. I'm not saying you can't get anywhere from the language model. I'm saying it's not obviously the right starting point, and I don't think it's a good bet.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no ground truth about what someone would write, but it does not state that prior knowledge needs a ground truth as the basis for an initial belief.

r002.rationale: It says learning from experience requires a goal and that, without one, there is no right thing for a language model to say.

r003.rationale: It mentions reward in reinforcement learning, but does not clearly identify reward as the criterion for what counts as the right action.

r004.rationale: It explains that an agent predicts what will happen, then can be wrong when events unfold and correct itself.

r005.rationale: It contrasts predicting what a person would say with predicting what will happen, but does not specifically discuss predicting how an interlocutor responds to the model’s own utterances.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it gives you a prior for imitating people. The question is how useful that is for learning what to do from the consequences of your own actions. Those are different problems.

If you train on what people say, the signal is: did you predict what the person would say next? It’s not: did your action lead to a better outcome? You can get very good at the first without ever confronting the second. And having read descriptions of people learning from experience isn’t the same as having a mechanism that learns from experience yourself.

I’m not saying imitation is useless. It can give you a starting policy, and language can convey useful knowledge. But you still have to establish that the starting point helps an agent continually improve through interaction with the world. That doesn’t follow just from its ability to produce impressive answers.

What I want is a system whose behavior is shaped by what happens to it—one that can discover something people don’t already know, try it, and get better because it worked. Imitation alone doesn’t give you that process.

r001.rationale: It discusses imitation as a starting policy, but does not state that prior knowledge requires ground truth to serve as an initial belief.

r002.rationale: It contrasts predicting what people say with improving outcomes, but does not argue that without a goal there is no defined right thing for a language model to say.

r003.rationale: It mentions better outcomes and actions, but does not identify reward as the criterion for the right action in reinforcement learning.

r004.rationale: It says agents should improve through interaction, but does not explain that world-model predictions can be checked against subsequent events.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss predictions of how an interlocutor will respond to the model's own utterances.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would question what you mean by a good prior. A prior for predicting what a person will say next? Certainly. But learning from experience is a different problem. You take an action, something happens, and you change your behavior in order to get more reward. The important thing is that your actions affect the experience you receive.

In imitation learning, somebody else has already chosen the actions. You’re learning to reproduce those choices. That can give you a useful starting policy, but it doesn’t necessarily give you the ability to improve that policy. In particular, it doesn’t teach you how to explore, how to assign credit for an outcome, or how to recognize that doing something different would be better.

So I wouldn’t say imitation can’t help. Of course it can help. What I object to is treating success at imitation as evidence that we’ve solved the central problem of intelligence. The central problem is how to learn from your own interaction with the world and go beyond what somebody has shown you.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes next-word prediction from learning through action, but does not say that prior knowledge requires ground truth as an initial belief.

r002.rationale: It discusses reward-guided behavior, but does not state that without a goal there is no defined right thing for a language model to say.

r003.rationale: It says actions can be changed to get more reward, but does not identify reward as the criterion for what counts as the right action in reinforcement learning.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss world-model predictions being checked against what subsequently happens.

r005.rationale: It does not mention predicting how an interlocutor responds to the model's own utterances.
